title: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
gist: University of Minnesota researchers vitrified pig kidneys to -150 C, kept one for over a year, then rewarmed them with iron oxide nanoparticles and an electromagnetic field and showed they regain blood flow and make urine. The results are a preprint, the organs show injury from toxic cryoprotectants, and long-term survival is unproven.

insights.claim: Pig kidneys cooled to -150 C and stored for months, one for just over a year, were rewarmed, regained color and made urine when tested on perfusion machines and transplanted into pigs, a first for a whole organ of this size.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A step toward indefinite organ banking, but based on a preprint without peer review and short-term (two hour) transplant monitoring.
insights.locator: Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150

insights.claim: The method loads the kidney with cryoprotectant, infuses iron oxide nanoparticles, cools it with cold nitrogen vapor to a glass-like state at about -120 C, then to -150 C, and rewarms it by activating the nanoparticles with an electromagnetic field to heat the organ uniformly, speeding up once it passes -120 C.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Nanoparticle-based uniform rewarming is the enabling technology; IP and scale-up from this platform are the thing to watch.

insights.claim: The same team vitrified rat kidneys in 2023 with storage up to 100 days, and moving to pig kidneys (about 100 times heavier, roughly 100 g versus 1 g) required re-engineering the cryoprotectant cocktail, taking three years.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Scaling to human-size organs is nontrivial; expect multi-year timelines for each size step.
insights.locator: The researchers successfully vitrified rat kidneys

insights.claim: Human organs can currently be preserved only 24 to 36 hours, which limits matching organs to recipients, and long-term banking could also let doctors prepare recipients' immune systems to reduce rejection and lifelong immunosuppressant side effects.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Longer preservation would reshape transplant logistics and could cut organ waste; a long-dated opportunity for transplant and preservation-tech companies.
insights.quote: instead of the patients waiting for the organ, it’s the organs that are waiting for the patients

insights.claim: Storing organs for a year would let organ banks supply emergency cases that cannot wait, such as some drug overdoses or gunshot wounds, according to the CEO of organ procurement organization LifeGift.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Defines an early use case for on-demand banked organs.
insights.locator: It’s a very big deal to go a year

insights.claim: The rewarmed kidneys produced around two-thirds of expected urine and showed injury attributed to the toxic cryoprotectant chemicals, and cryobiologist Greg Fahy says the experiments cannot show whether they would have supported life.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Do not treat this as clinical readiness; the key unresolved risk is toxicity and long-term function.
insights.quote: This is one big breakthrough that solves half the problem

insights.claim: Next steps are longer-duration pig transplant tests, a search for less toxic cryoprotectants, and experiments with human kidneys, with the lead surgeon expecting human kidneys may cope better than pig kidneys.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Watch for longer-term survival data and human organ trials as milestone catalysts.
insights.locator: The next step will be to test the kidneys in pigs
